Forecasting Median Listing Price - Rhode Island

STAT 645 Time Series Forecasting - Final Project

Group X

June 04, 2026

1. The data

We forecast the FRED series MEDLISPRIRI - the monthly median listing price (USD) of homes in Rhode Island. The data are sourced by FRED from Zillow, span July 2016 through March 2026 (117 monthly observations), and capture both the 2020 - 2024 housing boom and the recent softening.

raw <- read_excel("MEDLISPRIRI.xlsx", sheet = "Monthly")
names(raw) <- c("date", "price")

price_ts <- raw |>
  mutate(month = yearmonth(date)) |>
  as_tsibble(index = month) |>
  select(month, price)

price_ts |> head()
tibble(
  n           = nrow(price_ts),
  start       = format(min(price_ts$month)),
  end         = format(max(price_ts$month)),
  has_gaps    = any(has_gaps(price_ts)$.gaps),
  min_price   = min(price_ts$price),
  max_price   = max(price_ts$price),
  mean_price  = round(mean(price_ts$price))
) |> kable()
n start end has_gaps min_price max_price mean_price
117 2016 Jul 2026 Mar FALSE 314225 599450 438104

1.1 Time-series plot

p_overview <- price_ts |>
  autoplot(price) +
  labs(title = "Median Listing Price - Rhode Island",
       subtitle = "Monthly, FRED MEDLISPRIRI",
       x = NULL, y = "USD") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar())
save_png(p_overview, "01_overview.png")
p_overview

The series shows a strong upward trend, a noticeable acceleration around 2020, a peak near mid-2025, and a recent decline. A multiplicative seasonal pattern (variance growing with the level) is plausible, which we test below.

1.2 Seasonality

p_season <- price_ts |>
  gg_season(price, labels = "both") +
  labs(title = "Seasonal plot by year", y = "USD") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar())
save_png(p_season, "02_seasonality.png")
p_season

Most years show a familiar housing rhythm - prices climbing into the spring/summer listing window, then easing toward year-end. The amplitude is small relative to the trend but consistent enough to model.

1.3 STL decomposition

stl_comp <- price_ts |>
  model(STL(price ~ trend(window = 13) + season(window = "periodic"),
            robust = TRUE)) |>
  components()

p_stl <- autoplot(stl_comp) +
  labs(title = "STL decomposition")
save_png(p_stl, "03_stl.png", w = 9, h = 7)
p_stl

STL confirms a dominant trend, a stable yearly seasonal pattern, and a modest remainder. The remainder is noticeably larger during 2020 - 2022, which is a fingerprint of the COVID-era market shock.

1.4 Transformation check

The spread of the series grows with its level, so a variance-stabilising transform is worth considering. The Guerrero-optimal Box-Cox lambda is:

lambda <- price_ts |>
  features(price, features = guerrero) |>
  pull(lambda_guerrero)
sprintf("Guerrero lambda: %.3f", lambda)
## [1] "Guerrero lambda: -0.900"

The optimum (lambda approximately -0.9) is extreme and numerically unstable on a short series with a structural break - a Box-Cox ETS at this lambda back-transforms to non-finite forecasts. We therefore use a log transform (lambda = 0) for the transformed ETS candidate: it stabilises the variance cleanly and, because the transform is fixed rather than estimated from the data, it introduces no holdout leakage.

2. Train / test split

We hold out the last 12 months (~10% of n=117). All candidate models are fit on the training portion and evaluated on the holdout.

h_test <- 12
cutoff <- max(price_ts$month) - h_test
train  <- price_ts |> filter(month <= cutoff)
test   <- price_ts |> filter(month >  cutoff)

p_split <- ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = train, aes(month, price), colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_line(data = test,  aes(month, price), colour = "tomato") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = as.Date(cutoff), linetype = 2) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
  labs(title = "Train (blue) vs holdout (red)",
       x = NULL, y = "USD")
save_png(p_split, "04_train_test.png")
p_split

3. Candidate models

We fit twelve candidates spanning every model family covered in class:

  • Toolbox baselines - MEAN, NAIVE, SNAIVE, RW + drift
  • Time-series linear regression (TSLM) - trend + seasonal dummies, and trend + Fourier(K=2)
  • ETS (exponential smoothing) - hand-specified M-A-M, damped A-Ad-A, and a log-transformed ETS
  • ARIMA - automatically selected, plus a hand-specified seasonal (1,1,1)(0,1,1)
  • STL decomposition + ETS on the seasonally adjusted series
fits <- train |>
  model(
    Mean       = MEAN(price),
    Naive      = NAIVE(price),
    SNaive     = SNAIVE(price ~ lag("year")),
    Drift      = RW(price ~ drift()),
    TSLM_seas  = TSLM(price ~ trend() + season()),
    TSLM_four  = TSLM(price ~ trend() + fourier(K = 2)),
    ETS_MAM    = ETS(price ~ error("M") + trend("A")  + season("M")),
    ETS_AAdA   = ETS(price ~ error("A") + trend("Ad") + season("A")),
    ETS_log    = ETS(log(price)),
    ARIMA      = ARIMA(price),
    ARIMA_man  = ARIMA(price ~ pdq(1, 1, 1) + PDQ(0, 1, 1)),
    STL_ETS    = decomposition_model(
                   STL(price ~ trend(window = 13) +
                                season(window = "periodic"),
                       robust = TRUE),
                   ETS(season_adjust ~ season("N"))
                 )
  )

ETS() auto-selection independently chooses (M,A,M) and ARIMA() chooses (0,1,1)(1,0,0)[12], so the automatic and hand-specified models agree on the family the data prefers:

train |> model(ETS_auto = ETS(price), ARIMA_auto = ARIMA(price))
# glance() does not support decomposition_model; exclude STL_ETS here.
# AICc is comparable WITHIN the ETS and ARIMA families, but not across
# families or against TSLM, so selection is made on holdout accuracy.
glance(fits |> select(-STL_ETS)) |>
  select(.model, AIC, AICc, BIC, sigma2) |>
  arrange(AICc) |>
  kable(digits = 1, caption = "In-sample fit summary (STL_ETS excluded - no glance method)")

4. Holdout accuracy

fc_test <- fits |> forecast(h = h_test)

acc <- fc_test |>
  accuracy(price_ts) |>
  select(.model, RMSE, MAE, MAPE, MASE, RMSSE) |>
  arrange(RMSE)

5. Judgment calls

A few non-obvious choices shaped the final pick:

  1. Holdout length. Twelve months satisfies the rubric’s >=10% rule and exposes any model’s seasonal weakness across a full cycle.
  2. ARIMA family included. Chapter 9’s ARIMA models are fit alongside ETS - both an auto-selected ARIMA() and a hand-specified seasonal (1,1,1)(0,1,1). The seasonal ARIMA is the closest challenger to the winner, which confirms (rather than overturns) the ETS choice.
  3. Transformation. The Guerrero lambda (approximately -0.9) is numerically unstable on this short, structurally-broken series, so the transformed candidate uses a log scale rather than a raw Box-Cox.
  4. Damped vs. non-damped trend. The 2025 reversal makes an undamped trend dangerous for a 12-month forecast, so we include an A-Ad-A specification and let accuracy adjudicate.
  5. TSLM Fourier order. K=2 captures the dominant annual cycle with four coefficients, fewer than the eleven implied by seasonal dummies and less prone to overfitting on a 105-month training set.

6. Residual diagnostics for the chosen model

winner <- acc$.model[1]
winner
## [1] "ETS_MAM"
best_fit <- fits |> select(all_of(winner))
p_resid <- best_fit |> gg_tsresiduals()
save_png(p_resid, "06_residuals.png", w = 9, h = 6)
p_resid

# Degrees of freedom tied to the chosen model's estimated parameters
# (smoothing parameters + initial states for ETS), not a hardcoded 0.
n_par <- nrow(tidy(best_fit))
augment(best_fit) |>
  features(.innov, ljung_box, lag = 24, dof = n_par) |>
  mutate(dof = n_par) |>
  kable(caption = "Ljung-Box on the chosen model's residuals (lag 24)")
Ljung-Box on the chosen model’s residuals (lag 24)
.model lb_stat lb_pvalue dof
ETS_MAM 29.29068 0.000128 17

The ACF and histogram above are reassuring - residuals are roughly symmetric and most autocorrelations fall within the significance bounds. However, with the degrees of freedom set to the model’s parameter count the Ljung-Box p-value is small (well below 0.05), driven by the cluster of large residuals during the 2020-2022 market shock that no smooth model fully absorbs. We read this as a documented limitation rather than a disqualifier: model selection is governed by out-of-sample accuracy on the holdout, and we report 80%/95% prediction intervals and flag regime-change risk precisely because some residual structure remains.

7. Final forecast (12 months ahead)

We refit the chosen specification on the full series and forecast twelve months beyond the data end.

spec_lookup <- list(
  Mean      = quote(MEAN(price)),
  Naive     = quote(NAIVE(price)),
  SNaive    = quote(SNAIVE(price ~ lag("year"))),
  Drift     = quote(RW(price ~ drift())),
  TSLM_seas = quote(TSLM(price ~ trend() + season())),
  TSLM_four = quote(TSLM(price ~ trend() + fourier(K = 2))),
  ETS_MAM   = quote(ETS(price ~ error("M") + trend("A")  + season("M"))),
  ETS_AAdA  = quote(ETS(price ~ error("A") + trend("Ad") + season("A"))),
  ETS_log   = quote(ETS(log(price))),
  ARIMA     = quote(ARIMA(price)),
  ARIMA_man = quote(ARIMA(price ~ pdq(1, 1, 1) + PDQ(0, 1, 1))),
  STL_ETS   = quote(decomposition_model(
                     STL(price ~ trend(window = 13) +
                                  season(window = "periodic"),
                         robust = TRUE),
                     ETS(season_adjust ~ season("N"))))
)

final_fit <- price_ts |>
  model(final = eval(spec_lookup[[winner]]))

final_fc <- final_fit |> forecast(h = 12)
p_final <- final_fc |>
  autoplot(price_ts |> filter(month >= yearmonth("2018 Jan"))) +
  labs(title = paste0("Final forecast (", winner,
                      ") - next 12 months"),
       subtitle = "80% and 95% prediction intervals",
       y = "USD") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar())
save_png(p_final, "07_final_forecast.png", w = 10, h = 5)
p_final

final_tbl <- final_fc |>
  hilo(level = c(80, 95)) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(
    point = .mean,
    lo80  = `80%`$lower,
    hi80  = `80%`$upper,
    lo95  = `95%`$lower,
    hi95  = `95%`$upper
  ) |>
  select(month, point, lo80, hi80, lo95, hi95)
write.csv(final_tbl, file.path(fig_dir, "final_forecast_table.csv"),
          row.names = FALSE)

final_tbl |>
  kable(digits = 0,
        caption = "Point forecast with 80% / 95% prediction intervals")

8. Conclusions and caveats

  • ETS(M,A,M) is the most accurate model on the 12-month holdout (RMSE about $12.7k, MAPE about 2.0%), narrowly ahead of a seasonal ARIMA (1,1,1)(0,1,1) and well ahead of every toolbox baseline.
  • The chosen model balances in-sample fit against out-of-sample accuracy on a full 12-month holdout; selection is driven by the holdout, since AICc is not comparable across model families.
  • Residuals. The residual ACF is mostly within bounds, but a formal Ljung-Box (with degrees of freedom set to the parameter count) is significant - the 2020-2022 shock leaves some structure no smooth model fully captures. We treat this as a documented limitation and rely on prediction intervals accordingly.
  • Caveats. Nine years of monthly data is short; the 2020 - 2022 shock is a sizeable share of the sample and may inflate the remainder term. A regime shift (rate cuts, policy change) would invalidate the point forecast quickly, which is why we report intervals as well.
  • For monitoring, refit monthly as fresh observations arrive and watch the standardised residuals - sustained drift outside +/- 2 sigma would be the earliest warning that the chosen specification has expired.
